name: Tongkat ali
lead: Tongkat ali (Eurycoma longifolia, also called longjack or Malaysian ginseng) is a Southeast Asian shrub whose root is used in traditional medicine as an aphrodisiac and fever remedy and is sold worldwide as a dietary supplement marketed as a natural testosterone booster.[1][2][3][25] People in bodybuilding and looksmaxxing communities take it hoping for a chain that runs from higher testosterone to better libido, training drive and recovery, and then a leaner, more muscular physique and the masculine-looking features that appearance-focused users associate with higher androgens.[8][7][35]

The root contains quassinoids such as eurycomanone and alkaloids such as canthin-6-ones and beta-carbolines; about 65 compounds have been isolated from it.[3][26][25] Proposed mechanisms rest on laboratory and rat studies of the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis and steroidogenic enzymes.[17][18]

In human research, a 2022 meta-analysis of randomised trials found that E. longifolia supplementation was associated with higher serum total testosterone, with the authors noting a stronger effect in hypogonadal and aging men.[4] A 2024 systematic review of 27 proposed testosterone boosters concluded that most do not raise total testosterone against placebo and counted E. longifolia among agents with three studies.[5] A meta-analysis of two randomised trials found no significant overall erectile-function improvement, with gains in men whose baseline scores were lower.[6] Members of looksmax.org and T Nation disagree on how large any effect is compared with testosterone replacement or anabolic steroids.[7][8][34]

paras: Eurycoma longifolia is a slow-growing evergreen shrub or small tree of the family Simaroubaceae, native to Southeast Asia including Malaysia, Indonesia and Vietnam. It can reach about 10 m, is often unbranched, has large compound leaves with 30 to 40 leaflets, and is dioecious, growing in the understory of lowland forest.[1][25] The root is the part used medicinally.[1]

The common Malay name translates as 'Ali's walking stick'; Indonesian and Vietnamese names include pasak bumi and bach benh ('hundred ailments'), and other names such as penawar pahit mean 'bitter medicine' and refer to the root's bitterness.[1][25][31] Reviews of traditional use list antimalarial, aphrodisiac, antidiabetic, antimicrobial and antipyretic applications, with decoctions made from roots, leaves and fruit for different complaints.[2][3]

In Southeast Asian folk medicine the root decoction has been used as a tonic, aphrodisiac and fever remedy, including for malaria. A systematic review of antimicrobial and antiparasitic activity (20 articles selected, 17 showing potential) links laboratory findings to its traditional use for jaundice and malaria, and screening of Cambodian plants and isolation studies examined its antiplasmodial constituents.[1][2][9][26][27][30]

Standardised water-soluble root extracts, including branded products such as Physta (also sold as LJ100), are marketed for testosterone support, libido, energy and body composition.[1][4][33] Bodybuilders and athletes use it, believing it raises testosterone and performance, according to Wikipedia.[25] T Nation articles describe longjack as an ingredient for men's testosterone and sexual function, and a forum thread asked whether it benefits men on testosterone replacement.[32][33][34] A US-listed product label combines tongkat ali with chicken essence powder.[10]

Isolation work in the 1990s and 2000s identified quassinoid diterpenoids (including eurycomanone), canthin-6-one alkaloids and beta-carboline alkaloids from the root; one 2004 study characterised 65 compounds and screened them for cytotoxic, anti-HIV and antimalarial activity.[27][26][3] Eurycomanone (pasakbumin-A) is the main quassinoid, and a 2014 paper reported NF-kB inhibitors from the plant.[18][29][37] Wikipedia notes that as of 2022 no studies had examined isolated eurycomanone in humans.[37]

The proposed mechanisms come largely from animal and laboratory work. Standardised quassinoid-rich extracts improved spermatogenesis and fertility in male rats via the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis, and eurycomanone has been reported to inhibit phosphodiesterase and aromatase activity in steroidogenesis.[17][18] Human trial authors suggest testosterone increases may arise from activation of the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal and/or adrenal axes, mainly in older adults and nonhealthy populations.[13] A 2012 paper asked whether a standardised extract could be a testosterone booster for late-onset hypogonadism, and a 2000 review put E. longifolia among herbs with inconsistent results in sexual-dysfunction research.[19][28]

The 2022 systematic review and meta-analysis (nine studies in the review, five randomised trials in the meta-analysis) reported a pooled standardised mean difference of 1.35 in total testosterone with E. longifolia, a significant increase confirmed in the hypogonadism subgroup; trials were small and included both healthy volunteers and men with low testosterone.[4]

A 2024 systematic review of 52 studies of 27 proposed testosterone boosters reported that most failed to increase total testosterone versus placebo, with exceptions including beta-hydroxy beta-methylbutyrate and betaine for male athletes; it included three E. longifolia studies and discussed E. longifolia, a pomegranate-cacao blend and a purified shilajit extract in its findings.[5]

A 6-month randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled four-arm trial in 45 men (average age about 47) with androgen deficiency of aging males found erectile function improved in both interventions, with the best results in men combining 200 mg of E. longifolia with concurrent training.[11] A related randomised trial examined exercise with or without E. longifolia on strength and cardiorespiratory fitness in men with androgen deficiency.[12] A randomised trial of 32 healthy young men examined the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal and adrenal axes.[13] A 2015 meta-analysis of two randomised trials (139 participants) found no significant overall difference in IIEF-5 at 12 weeks, with an improvement of about 2 points among those with lower baseline scores.[6] A randomised trial examined immune markers in middle-aged adults using a standardised extract.[14] Wikipedia states that clinical research has not found a significant effect as a supplement and that it is under preliminary study for erectile dysfunction and immunomodulation.[25]

A 2010 review noted that although toxicity and safety evaluation studies had been carried out, a major gap remained in the scientific basis for commercial use and consumer safety clearance of tongkat ali products.[2] Reported side effects in Wikipedia's summary include nausea, stomach discomfort, diarrhea and headaches; rare liver injury has been reported, mostly in bodybuilders, and use in pregnancy is not recommended.[25] A randomised pharmacokinetic study reported that an E. longifolia water extract modified propranolol bioavailability, indicating the potential for interaction with some drugs.[15] A New Zealand primary-care article on tongkat ali (long jack) is also available.[16] A comprehensive adverse-event profile has not been established.

Tongkat ali has been sold in the bodybuilding supplement market since at least the early 2000s: in 2003 T Nation's store promoted a product whose active ingredient was described as pharmaceutical-grade Eurycoma longifolia, and forum members at the time circulated botanical and ethnobotanical notes about it.[20][31] T Nation later published longjack articles and a guide on sex and testosterone supplements, and promoted the branded LJ100 extract.[32][33][35] On looksmax.org, threads ask whether it lowers or raises DHT, whether it is 'cope' compared with SARMs or steroids, and promote it as 'backed by studies'.[7][8][21]

Wikipedia reports that in 2006 the US FDA banned seven products containing undeclared prescription drugs or analogues, that two coffee brands were recalled in 2017 for hidden erectile-dysfunction drug ingredients, and that a 2004 Malaysian study found 36 percent of more than 200 registered products exceeded legal mercury limits.[25] Extract labels such as 1:50 or 1:200 are difficult to verify, and a Malaysian technical guideline recommended eurycomanone as a standardisation marker.[25]

Harvesting the root kills the plant. Malaysia restricts raw exports and wild harvesting, and in 2016 a minister warned the species could become extinct within 20 years without faster cultivation; the IUCN listed it as Least Concern in 2024.[25]

Human studies include a 2022 meta-analysis of randomised trials on total testosterone,[4] a 2024 systematic review of testosterone boosters,[5] a 2015 meta-analysis on erectile function,[6] a 6-month randomised trial in androgen-deficient men,[11] a randomised trial of exercise with or without E. longifolia on strength and fitness,[12] a randomised trial in healthy young men,[13] a randomised immunomodulation trial,[14] and a pharmacokinetic interaction trial with propranolol.[15] Registered trials include an erectile-dysfunction study of a tongkat ali plus maca product (n=197) and a small intimacy study.[22][36] Animal studies include libido and semen work in boars and sleep consolidation in mice.[23][24]

lore.intro: Tongkat ali is a staple of 'natural test' stacks on looksmax.org and T Nation. Discussion ranges from enthusiastic summaries of trials to scepticism about whether any legal supplement matters.[7][8][21]

claims.believers: A looksmax.org post says studies show it increases total and free testosterone by lowering SHBG and cites a 200 mg/day trial reporting about a 37 percent rise.[8]
claims.experts: A 2022 meta-analysis of randomised trials reported a significant pooled increase in total testosterone, strongest in hypogonadal and aging men, while a 2024 review of 27 boosters found most do not raise total testosterone.[4][5]

claims.claim: Tongkat ali improves libido and erectile function
claims.believers: Forum posts and supplement marketing describe it as an aphrodisiac and energy aid, in line with its traditional reputation.[8][20]
claims.experts: A 2015 meta-analysis of two trials found no significant overall improvement in IIEF-5 at 12 weeks, though men with lower baseline scores improved, and a 6-month trial in men with androgen deficiency reported better erectile function with E. longifolia plus training.[6][11]

claims.claim: Tongkat ali lowers cortisol and improves body composition
claims.believers: The same looksmax.org post says modern research backs reduced cortisol and improved body composition.[8]
claims.experts: A randomised trial examined effects on strength and cardiorespiratory fitness in androgen-deficient men, and a trial in healthy young men examined hormone regulation; pooled results for cortisol or body composition are not available.[12][13]

claims.claim: Natural testosterone from tongkat ali rivals or beats injected testosterone
claims.believers: One looksmax.org reply asserts that '1000 ng/dl natural testosterone mogs any amount of synthetic testosterone'; another says any legal supplement has negligible results on its own.[8][7]
claims.experts: No published trial has compared tongkat ali with testosterone replacement or anabolic steroids; the 2024 review concluded most testosterone boosters fail to raise total testosterone.[5]

claims.claim: It is a legal, low-risk alternative to steroids.
claims.believers: Forum threads present it as a 'natural test' option, and T Nation material promotes standardised extracts as a way to raise testosterone.[7][33]
claims.experts: Wikipedia reports rare liver injury mostly in bodybuilders and documented adulterated products; a 2010 review noted a gap in safety evidence for commercial products.[25][2]

claims.claim: It raises DHT and affects hair.
claims.believers: A looksmax.org thread asks whether tongkat ali lowers or boosts DHT, reflecting concern about hair loss on androgen-raising supplements.[21]
claims.experts: No published trial has reported DHT or hair outcomes with E. longifolia.[4][13]

claims.claim: Only the right branded extract works.
claims.believers: T Nation material says longjack boosts natural testosterone if the right kind, LJ100, is sourced.[33]
claims.experts: Wikipedia notes that extract ratios on labels are hard to verify and recommends marker compounds for standardisation; trials of standardised water extracts such as Physta exist for immune markers and hormones.[25][14]

claims.believers: A T Nation thread discusses whether it adds anything for men on testosterone replacement, citing rat studies of castrated animals.[34]
claims.experts: No human trial has tested E. longifolia alongside testosterone replacement.[4][5]

card.summary: Southeast Asian root extract sold as a 'natural test booster'; small trials lean positive, but broader reviews are sceptical.
card.aka: Eurycoma longifolia; longjack; Malaysian ginseng; LJ100
card.note: Trials are small and results differ between reviews; one study found it altered propranolol bioavailability.

quick.overview:
Tongkat ali is a Southeast Asian root used traditionally as an aphrodisiac and now sold as a testosterone-support supplement. It is popular in bodybuilding and looksmaxxing circles.
A 2022 meta-analysis of small randomised trials found higher total testosterone with E. longifolia, especially in men with low levels, but a 2024 review of 27 testosterone boosters concluded most do not raise total testosterone, and erectile-function results are mixed.
quick.mechanism: Lab and rat studies suggest its quassinoids act on the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis and on steroidogenic enzymes; forum posts also claim it lowers SHBG, which is not confirmed.
quick.risks: Safety data are limited; a 2010 review noted gaps in safety evidence for commercial products, and one study found a water extract changed propranolol absorption. It is sold as a supplement, so product content varies.

angle.text: Users take standardised tongkat ali extract as a legal add-on to training, aiming for higher testosterone and better energy, mood and libido, which they connect to recovery and body composition. Trials in men with low testosterone are the main human data.
